Two edge cases in ask_trinity (ent#328/#1981), found by /edge-cases. (1) truncate cut on UTF-16 CODE UNITS, so a boundary landing inside a surrogate pair left an unpaired surrogate - ill-formed Unicode that a strict UTF-8 encoder or JSON-RPC client replaces with U+FFFD or rejects; proven by construction (65,536-char answer with U+1F600 straddling the cut). Fixed by stepping back one unit off a high surrogate; only the final unit can be orphaned, so one check covers it. (2) The context-loss warning lived inside `if (responseSessionId)`, so a 200 that answered but OMITTED session_id produced no warning at all and the caller silently lost its conversation context - exactly what that warning exists to prevent; the 'different id returned' branch was covered and the neighbouring 'no id returned' one was not. The warning is now decided by the REQUEST's session, with distinct wording since 'a new session was started' is false when none came back. Both fixes are mirrored into src/helper-mcp/src/client.ts, which carries a byte-identical copy. Covers: the straddling cut, the limit still reported as the ORIGINAL max, a fully-fitting pair surviving, a BMP-only answer still cut at exactly max (the step-back must not misfire), a short answer untouched, the 200-char ERROR-path truncation (likelier to meet arbitrary bytes than the answer path), and all four session shapes. Two rows were also added to the existing PARITY_CASES table: mutating ONLY the helper copy previously changed nothing in the suite - the parity claim held just for the cases in its table - and both helper-only mutations now fail it.

deploy-local validated an archive-supplied .mcp.json 32 lines AFTER shutil.copytree(extract_root, dest_path), and the finally block removed only temp_dir - so a config the ent#213 validator refused stayed on disk under /data/deployed-templates/<version_name>/, a live member of crud._LOCAL_TEMPLATE_ROOTS, addressable by the same caller via POST /api/agents {template: local:<version_name>}. A guard that runs after the persist is not a gate. Fix: the guard moved to step 6a, running on extract_root before the copy AND before the quota check and the stop-previous-version step (a doomed deploy no longer stops a running agent on its way to a 400), plus _remove_partial_deploy as a second layer for failures between copytree and create_agent_fn (_prepopulate_workspace_from_template's 500) - deliberately handed over before creation starts, since a directory a container may already reference must not be removed on a late failure. ent#213's suite tests _validate_archive_mcp_config in isolation ('the full deploy flow needs Docker'), which is exactly why the ordering was never covered; these drive the REAL deploy_local_agent_logic and assert on the filesystem, needing no Docker because the rejection path now reaches nothing external. Covers: the issue's reproduction, local:<name> resolving to nothing, the ordering pinned twice (behaviourally by exploding every post-guard step, and statically by source order - the behavioural residue assertion alone cannot distinguish the two candidate fixes once cleanup exists), the valid path reaching creation with the template in place, an archive with no .mcp.json, and both sides of the cleanup boundary.

PULL_MODE_PILOT_AGENTS can only route agent-to-agent work (#2048). _AUTONOMOUS_TRIGGERS declares seven triggers autonomous and pull_owns_dispatch consulted all seven, but capacity_manager only offers a row to the durable queue when its producer passed overflow_policy='queue_persistent', and exactly one of the three producers does: task_execution_service uses 'reject' (scheduler/ALL cron + fan-out), dispatch_admission_service uses 'queue_in_memory' (sequential chat, human chat), only chat_execution_service (POST /task) uses 'queue_persistent'. So on a cron-driven agent the pilot flag is INERT and #1766's soak measures nothing - silently, because the gate sits behind an overflow_policy short-circuit, so for a schedule row pull_owns_dispatch is never called at all and the row is pushed indistinguishably from the flag being unset, while PULL_MIGRATION_TESTING.md section 9 M1 told the operator to go check an env var that is present and correct. Issue decision was Option 1 (make the reach honest, do not extend it). Corrects the issue's own table: the reachable set is {agent, event}, not {agent} - #1578's task-completion loopback POSTs to the same /task route and is tagged 'event' via an internal-secret-gated X-Event-Trigger, with no capacity bypass. Tests pin: the reach set derived from what _derive_task_trigger can emit rather than hardcoded; every autonomous trigger classified as reachable or stranded so a new one cannot join the stranded set unreviewed; the narrowing is a runtime NO-OP over the only producer that consults the predicate (it stops a false claim, it does not change a verdict); and note_unreachable_pull_trigger reports a stranded row once per (agent, trigger), never for a non-pilot / reachable / interactive trigger, and never raises. A structural guard asserts the three producers' overflow_policy literals, so implementing the deferred Option 2 (wiring cron to queue_persistent) fails this test and forces PULL_REACHABLE_TRIGGERS and section 9's prose to be revisited in the same change - a silently-stale reach set being exactly the bug. Also updates test_1766: its 'pilot owns EVERY autonomous trigger' case asserted reach the system never had (it passed only by calling the predicate outside the context that constrains it), and its producer-gate case drove a queue_persistent acquire carrying 'schedule' - a combination production cannot produce - now driven with 'agent', the shape that actually occurs. SUPERSEDED IN PART BY #2391: the structural guard fired as designed when Option 2 landed and was re-derived, not relaxed - task_execution_service now carries BOTH 'reject' and 'queue_persistent', and a second assertion pins that the wider one is reachable only through pull_owns_dispatch, which is the property #2048 could not assert and the one that keeps the blast radius equal to the pilot allowlist. The reachable set is now {agent, event, schedule, webhook, reminder} and the stranded set {loop, fan_out, a2a, operator_response}; see unit/test_2391_scheduled_pull_reach.py.

The free-text PAT scrubbers only fired on a literal `https://` (#2052) - the follow-up ent#347 predicted. `skill_source_clone._CREDENTIAL_URL_RE` was `https://[^\s/?#]+@`, anchored on the scheme, while the parse-based `utils.url_validation.strip_url_credentials` (ent#334) resolves an authority with no scheme at all. Three shapes therefore slipped past the regex and were echoed VERBATIM: protocol-relative `//tok@github.com/o/r`, the scheme-less shorthand `tok@github.com/o/r`, and an alternate scheme `git+ssh://tok@...` (plus the empty-userinfo `https://@host`, which the old `+` quantifier could not match). Reachable rather than theoretical: `_adopt_legacy_clone` writes source rows with no validation and `validate_skills_library_url` accepts the scheme-less form, so a stored URL may legitimately take them, and `_scrub_pat` then runs over `str(e)` of an ARBITRARY exception whose text is not constrained to what `_authenticated_url` built. Sink is `system_settings['skills_library_last_error']` - durable and admin-rendered. Fixed by moving the rule next to the parser as `scrub_url_credentials_in_text` rather than adding a fourth hand-written regex; `redact` delegates and `_CREDENTIAL_URL_RE` is deleted. The free-text side stays text-oriented on purpose - git stderr is prose plus several URLs, so there is no single URL to hand `urlparse`. Tests are mostly PARITY assertions over one shared corpus (the ent#334 cross-check shapes plus the three that regressed): the two must agree on the resolved authority, on WHETHER a credential is present at all (the actual defect), and no userinfo may survive. A structural test asserts `_CREDENTIAL_URL_RE` is gone so a local pattern cannot be reintroduced. Regression guards keep `?ref=a@b` untouched - the removed scheme anchor was also what kept the pattern off a query `@`, which is why the bare form carries a run-start boundary - plus multi-URL free text, idempotency and never-raises. 21 of these fail against the pre-fix scrubber, one with the token verbatim. Also pins the scan LINEAR: dropping the `https://` anchor also drops the literal `str.find` could jump to, and the first fix expressed the new rule as a class-first pattern, which rescanned a long no-`@` run from every offset - 24s on 200KB, 151s on 500KB, on RAW git stderr that is unbounded and partly remote-controlled, i.e. a DoS reachable from a hostile repo. Rewritten to walk maximal authority-legal runs; same 500KB now scrubs in 1.2ms.

TZ-capability packaging parity (#1823), #1891-shaped static guard. Both tz-resolving images (backend, scheduler) install `tzdata-legacy` AND declare the `tzdata` wheel; tests/requirements-test.txt declares it too (CI must not be MORE capable than production — that inversion kept this bug green on CI and red in the image for months); the base image's exemption is asserted against the reason that holds (its tree registers no CronTrigger) rather than inherited; and both images pin the SAME APScheduler exactly, since the #1472 contract ('reject exactly what the scheduler would') is only true while validator and executor build the same CronTrigger — a floor on either side does not merely risk drift, it produces it, as `>=3.10.0,<4.0.0` resolves to whatever is newest at build time. Stale-path guard. Comments are stripped before matching, so the fix's own explanatory comments cannot make the guard vacuous. Plus one runtime assertion resolving `Europe/Kiev` — the one that goes red INSIDE a mis-packaged image. Pure stdlib, no Docker.

`src/scheduler/service.py::_add_job` permanent-vs-transient classification (#1823 D5, a gap in #1472's own bounded-retry machinery). `zoneinfo.ZoneInfoNotFoundError` is a KeyError subclass, so it fell through to the transient arm and retried every 60s forever with a frozen next_run_at (canary E-06 fires on it). Both directions pinned: RuntimeError and a plain KeyError must STAY transient, because the permanent arm suppresses retries. Plus log-once bounding, the recovery path (a parked row registers and clears its flag once the runtime can resolve the zone), and one un-injected case registering a real legacy alias. Injected fake DB/scheduler, no Docker.

`PUT /api/agents/{name}/schedules/{id}` timezone gate (#1823 D4 — the silent persist that was quieter and worse than the create path's 500: the alias was written to the row and the failure deferred to a fire time that never came). Every case asserts the WRITE did not happen, not just the status code. Non-admin caller. Real-input (`Not/AZone`), fault-injected unresolvable-but-pytz-known, and a resolvable legacy alias going through with no injection. Route handler driven directly, no Docker.

Cron-only `PUT` validates against the row's OWN timezone instead of a hardcoded "UTC" (#1823) — the deliberate 200->400 for a row already storing an unregisterable zone. Pins assert on the ARGUMENT handed to the validator, since on a tz-complete runtime every zone validates identically and a verdict-based test would pass against the old literal. The injected failure misses exactly ONE zone for the same reason. Covers incoming-tz precedence, the NULL-stored-tz UTC fallback, the healthy path staying 200, and that a bad cron is still rejected. No Docker.

The pure registry.yaml parser (ent#14 / TMPL-002). Covers the happy path; `templates: []` treated as a SUCCESS rather than a failure, because an empty registry is the deliberate day-one state and classifying it as an error would serve stale entries forever; every document-level refusal; ent#314 YAML hardening reaching this document specifically (any single alias, a level-6 anchor bomb, duplicate keys, oversize - all refuse the WHOLE document and degrade to the bundled floor, never a partial parse); per-entry drops; dot path segments; case-insensitive duplicate repos; field caps; `priority: true` not sorting as 1 (a bool is an int in Python and used to 500 the router's sort); a bounded error list; and THE ALLOWLIST - 16 forbidden keys asserted absent from the frozen four-field record, so a hostile registry cannot inject fork_to_own, credentials, schedules, data_paths, persistent_state, skills, hidden or id.

Transport + cache for the remote registry (ent#14). The byte ceiling counts WIRE bytes via iter_raw (S1): a gzip bomb whose Content-Length passes the early abort is refused as encoding_refused with zero body bytes read, and peak allocation is asserted under 8 MB against 64 MB of decoded payload. Both transport fixtures convert every mock response to a REAL stream - a buffered httpx.Response(content=...) decodes in its constructor and marks the stream consumed, so it can only ever exercise iter_bytes(), which is precisely why the pre-S1 ceiling tests were green against a 1030:1 hole. Also: a LYING Content-Length re-probed through a second client to prove the lie was actually told (otherwise a future refactor that starts trusting the header stays green); early abort on a declared oversize length; connect/timeout/HTTP/redirect failures; HTML and binary bodies; URL-validation refusal never dialling; TTL + jitter; URL change; the cross-worker GENERATION bump (a per-process invalidate half-applies under --workers 2); serve-stale and its 7-day cap; negative caching; and the durable last-known-good (persist-on-change-only, cold-start restore, and rejection of a wrong-URL / older-parser / too-old / tampered row).

The fail-open MATRIX at the catalog seam (ent#14). The design rule is that a broken registry can only ever degrade to the bundled floor, never break the catalog - so every assertion is on the CATALOG OUTPUT, not on whether an except branch ran (a test asserting the branch ran still passes if the branch returns garbage). 19 failure modes x 2: catalog equality, and again through the ROUTER's own sort, where a non-int priority used to 500 the endpoint. Plus a registry service that simply RAISES; per-entry fencing; the full precedence ladder admin-override -> registry -> DEFAULT_GITHUB_TEMPLATE_REPOS including zero-requests-when-curated; the config hard kill switch beating the DB row; list/detail/create sharing ONE ladder (F1 - the second resolver feeds GET /api/templates/{id} AND agent creation, so a divergence changes what gets cloned); payload key-set equality; and a hostile registry failing to inject fork_to_own / credentials / schedules / hidden / id. Two tests exist to stop the matrix being vacuous: one pins that the real bundled floor is non-empty, one re-probes the lying header.

GET/PUT/DELETE /api/settings/template-registry on the real router (ent#14). The security assertion is the PRINCIPAL MATRIX: an admin-owned AGENT-scoped key passes assert_admin because it resolves to its owner carrying the owner's role (the trinity-ops-agent#232 trap), so both writes additionally require reject_agent_principal - otherwise any agent could repoint the platform's template registry. Also: audit rows on write AND on a no-op reset; partial update; the hard-kill-switch 409; and the catch-all 422 on BOTH generic write paths (PUT and DELETE /api/settings/{key}) for all four registry keys, so the SSRF gate has no second unvalidated write path. Route order versus the /{key} catch-all is pinned by test (Invariant #4).

All four owner/repo gates agree on a shared fixture corpus (ent#14). Compares BEHAVIOUR, not source strings - two of the copies already differ in character-class ordering, so a source diff would report drift that does not exist and miss drift that does. Pins one DELIBERATE divergence: `.` sits inside the character class in the three older copies, so `../evil` matches them, while the registry gate refuses dot segments outright; registry acceptance is therefore asserted to be a strict SUBSET of every other gate, which is the property that actually matters - the newest gate may be stricter but must never admit something an existing gate rejects.

The fork_to_own fail-closed gate (ent#14 F2 + S2). F2: a rate-limited (403) template.yaml read as fork_to_own=None skipped the gate and bound the agent to the SHARED upstream template repo instead of a user-owned copy. S2 is the sharper case - the gate decided from the CATALOG dict (global platform PAT, default branch, 600s process cache) while the correctly-credentialed creation read ran one line earlier. That failed in both directions at once: GitHub answers 404 (not 403) for a repo a token cannot see, so a PRIVATE fork_to_own: required template readable only by the creator's per-user PAT (ent#162, a supported flow) came back absent and the gate PASSED (false pass, no attacker involved); and a poisoned shared cache entry 503'd creators whose own PAT reads fine for the full TTL (false refuse). Both the availability verdict and the fork_to_own VALUE now come from the creation read, unioned with the catalog so the change can only remove a false pass. Driven through the REAL _resolve_template against a GitHub whose answer depends on which token asks. Verified red (measured 2026-08-05): neutralising the F2 guard fails 11 of 31; restoring the catalog-reading gate fails 3; and the plausible HALF-FIX - moving only the availability verdict while the value still comes from the catalog - still fails 1, so the suite is not vacuous against the fix that tests green.

SSRF gate on the template-registry URL (ent#14 S3): RFC 6598 shared address space (100.64.0.0/10) is reported by Python's ipaddress as neither is_private nor is_reserved, so the predicate stack admitted it — refused now, with both /10 boundaries held public so a legitimate registry is not blackholed, and one CGNAT record among public ones enough to refuse (every resolved record is checked). Also pins the neighbouring internal ranges, IPv4-mapped IPv6, the HTTPS-only and no-userinfo rules, and refusal (not pass-through) of an unresolvable host. DNS is stubbed — the property under test is the predicate, not the resolver. Also pins WHY the sibling validate_skills_library_url has no CGNAT clause and must not grow one as a consistency fix: it is allowlisted by HOST, so the operator never chooses a destination and the resolved address is not an operator-controlled input. Four non-allowlisted hosts (incl. the suffix lookalike github.com.evil.com and the real-but-unlisted raw.githubusercontent.com) are refused while resolving to a PUBLIC address, so the refusal provably does not come from the address predicates, plus the accept case so it is an allowlist and not a blanket refusal. Copying the clause across is harmless; deleting the registry one as redundant is not, and this is where that turns from a judgement call into a failure. Verified red: removing the CGNAT clause fails 5 of 33, widening the skills-library allowlist fails 4.

Compose/env packaging for the two registry knobs (ent#14), caught by /validate-pr before merge. config.py read TEMPLATE_REGISTRY_ENABLED / TEMPLATE_REGISTRY_URL and NEITHER compose file injected them; prod compose launches standalone (no base merge, no env_file) and is what every deploy path uses, so both were inert on any real instance. The var is the feature's HARD kill switch - the documented air-gap answer no system_settings row can override - so an inert one means default-ON outbound egress with no way to stop it. The irony is pinned in the docstring because it is the lesson: the config.py comment block directly above the os.getenv call argues at length against routing the flag through _resolve_bool_flag precisely because that helper's opt-in-only env leg would 'ship an inert kill switch (#1039 class)' - and it then shipped inert by the other route. Covers: injection present in BOTH composes; the ENABLED default is the ${VAR:-true} form and not a hardcoded true (which passes a presence check while re-breaking the switch); the URL default is the full non-empty https literal, since a bare :- arrives set-but-empty and shadows the code default (#1076 class) - worse than absent because it looks wired; compose and config.py defaults do not drift; dev/prod agree; both documented in .env.example. Sixth recurrence of the #1039/#1056 packaging-gap class (after #1056 VOIP_*, ent#31 LOG_*, #1039, #1871 AGENT_LOG_*, #411 CANARY_*), so it is pinned rather than trusted. Shape mirrors test_canary_env_prod_parity.py, the guard for the fifth. The meta-test proves the matcher fails on pre-fix content AND on a hardcoded value; the guard was additionally verified by deleting the real prod line and watching it go red - the first attempt at that proof used an unescaped grep -v whose $ read as an end-of-line anchor, matched nothing, and reported a false green.

The .trinity/ authored-vs-runtime split survives a backend Push (#2070). Every Push runs `git rm --cached` over tracked-but-now-ignored files; the fleet list ignored `.trinity/` WHOLESALE, so template-committed content there was untracked and its deletion pushed, guarded only by a hardcoded two-entry pathspec that was wrong three times (brain-orb ent#76, setup.sh — swept live — and pre-check #2070, the SCHED-COND-001 hook the platform's own docs tell authors to commit). Silent by construction: only the index is touched, so the working tree keeps running and the failure lands one re-clone/recreate later as an agent with no hook, whose every cron tick then runs a full LLM turn. Runs the REAL `_build_gitignore_merge_command` + `_build_rm_cached_ignored_command` against REAL git repos in tmp (the defect is in git's own descend/negation semantics, which a mocked container cannot express). Asserts the SPLIT, never the current exemption strings: 8 authored paths survive, 9 runtime files stay untracked, a fresh clone still RUNS the hook, the superseded wholesale line is replaced (append-only would be inert — git never descends into a dir-form exclusion), user rules merely mentioning .trinity are preserved, the merge is idempotent, exemptions are derived from `_TRINITY_AUTHORED_PATHS`, and a newly-invented runtime file needs no action. Mutation-verified 4 ways (wholesale ignore restored 5F, hardcoded exemptions 1F, no stale-line migration 2F, pre-check dropped from the set 4F).

The fleet-wide `.gitignore` merge now runs at agent CREATION (#2069). `_GITIGNORE_PATTERNS` was applied only on Push/init, never at creation, so a `github:` agent whose 15-min in-container auto-sync loop is on from birth (the GIT_SYNC_AUTO set — non-source/fork agents, ephemeral ghosts INCLUDED) auto-committed `.trinity/` runtime state and the root-level `.env`/`.mcp.json` into its user-owned repo before any Push could migrate the list. Loads the REAL git_service (heavy deps mocked) through crud.git_service so the predicate, merge builders and readiness poller are production code. (1) Merge behaviour (AC#2): the real `_build_gitignore_merge_command` output run against real tmp git repos — no-.gitignore template gets the full list, a partial one is preserved+completed, and after the merge a bare `git add -A` stages NONE of .env/.mcp.json/.trinity/*/content/*/.claude/projects while genuine code + the .gitignore itself ARE staged; #2070 authored hooks (.trinity/pre-check) stay includable. (2) Idempotence/#953 (AC#4): an EXACT-seed template committed to a bare origin shows no `M .gitignore`; run-twice is a no-op (no pattern duplicated); a stale wholesale `.trinity/` line yields a LEGITIMATE supersede→append edit (#2070) — proving the no-drift contract is scoped to already-canonical templates. (3) Readiness gating (AC#1/R1): merge_gitignore_after_clone waits while /health is down and times out cleanly with no exception; once ready ∧ .git present it runs `_build_gitignore_merge_command` against the toplevel and NEVER `_build_rm_cached_ignored_command` (creation is PREVENT, not REMEDIATE); skips a ready-but-no-.git failed clone and an unresolved `_git_toplevel` None; and a hung docker exec is `asyncio.wait_for`-bounded (a missing wrap would hang the test); and the readiness poll runs OUTSIDE `_gitignore_merge_semaphore` so a slow-/never-booting agent parked in its /health wait cannot head-of-line-block a healthy already-ready agent's Docker-exec merge — pinned with a 1-permit semaphore, since the pre-fix in-semaphore poll would deadlock the fast agent. (4) `_git_auto_sync_baked` matrix (R2): fork-to-own AND non-source AND ephemeral non-source github+PAT bake (the ghost is never operator-Pushed, so the merge MUST cover it — the predicate ignores config.ephemeral), while source-mode-non-fork, local/no-repo, no-PAT and ephemeral-source-mode do NOT — and `_materialize_agent_files` fires spawn_gitignore_merge_after_clone on EXACTLY that predicate (the AC#6 regression, real predicate flowing through crud). Round-trip property analysis of GITHUB_PAT propagation as merged by #1979. The contract is stated once as a Hypothesis property - after a rotation the agent reads back exactly the new token under all three key names (GITHUB_PAT/GH_TOKEN/GITHUB_TOKEN) - with the oracle being a byte-faithful copy of the agent-server's own last-wins .env parser, because what the agent sees is the only definition of success for a credential rotation. Plus idempotence, unrelated keys surviving, and the old token not surviving anywhere as text. Deterministic boundaries that hold: empty file, no trailing newline, leading whitespace/tab, commented-out line, present-but-empty, lookalike and prefixed keys, CRLF, append-not-glued. Three xfail(strict) findings: a duplicated GITHUB_PAT line survives count=1 and wins under last-wins parsing so the agent keeps the revoked token while the rotation reports updated (#2016); a backslash in the token raises re.error because the new line is used as an re.sub REPLACEMENT (#2017); and the writer escapes an embedded quote while the reader never unescapes it (#2017, a .env parse-contract issue deliberately left byte-faithful by #1999).

Credential injects mirrored every .env key into the long-lived agent-server process env, and all five runtime spawn sites (claude_code, headless_executor, codex_runtime, gemini_runtime x2) passed env={**os.environ, ...} - a one-way sync with NO delete phase. A key removed from .env by any non-mirroring write path (SSH, docker exec, or an agent editing its own .env) kept reaching every subsequently-spawned execution until container restart, and was invisible to /proc/<pid>/environ (an exec-time snapshot - runtime os.environ mutations never appear there) AND to docker exec (which shows the container baseline, not this process's mutated env), so credential revocation silently failed with no inspection route that could reveal it. Fix: services/execution_env.py rebuilds the execution env per spawn as INITIAL_ENV (boot baseline = what docker exec shows) + .env (parsed fresh, authoritative for credentials) + RUNTIME_OVERRIDES (#1089 token rotation - applied AFTER the file so a stale token in .env cannot beat an explicit rotation; None = force-unset, which a dict merge cannot express) + extra (EXECUTION_TAG_NAME last, #407). The process mirror gains a delete phase that restores the container baseline rather than popping blind, and only ever undoes keys it itself wrote. Covers: the issue's exact reproduction (inject, delete out-of-band, assert the next execution is clean), re-injecting a cleaned .env, baseline restore vs delete, the #1089 no-regression cases, EXECUTION_TAG_NAME non-displacement, tolerant .env parsing incl. the writer's own backslash escaping (.strip('"') eats a legitimate trailing quote), unreadable/oversized files degrading to the baseline rather than raising on the spawn path, protected keys (.env is agent-writable and now read at every spawn, so PATH/LD_PRELOAD/BASH_ENV redirection is refused), the name-only drift report added to /api/credentials/status, and a static guard that fails if a sixth spawn site reintroduces the {**os.environ} form.

GET /api/executions/timeline - bucketed fleet execution rollups (ent#326), the backend half of ent#94's grid-widget foundation so three tile sub-issues (#96/#98/#101) share one query instead of each growing their own. Time-series sibling of /api/executions/stats: same table, same access model, buckets instead of scalars. The central distinction the file pins is that an ANALYTICS AXIS cannot degrade the way a FILTER can - /stats and the list route coerce an unknown `hours` to 24, which is right for a filter (worst case: more rows than asked for) and wrong for a chart, where it silently redraws a window the caller never requested; so both params 422 by name. Covers: unknown group_by and unknown hours each rejected with a named 422 (incl. a SQL-ish group_by, since the key is interpolated into the GROUP BY); hours=0 refused for hour/day because an all-time axis emits one bucket per interval since the fleet's first execution, but ALLOWED for trigger/agent which have no continuum; gap-fill producing a continuous, ordered, duplicate-free UTC axis where a populated bucket keeps its values and neighbours are real zeros (a missing bucket and a zero bucket mean different things to a reader, #1107); categorical groupings NOT gap-filled (inventing empty agent buckets would invent agents); trigger folding done in Python through _TRIGGER_BUCKETS so an unmapped trigger lands in the explicit Other catch-all rather than vanishing, with same-bucket triggers summed and no execution lost. Access scoping mirrors /api/executions - the caller's list reaches the query, admin is None (no filter), and the dangerous direction is pinned directly: an empty allow-list returns an empty series, never everything. DB layer driven against a real SQLite table: agent scoping, 'error' counted as failed (so the chart cannot contradict the stat card above it), NULL cost/context coalesced to 0, window respected in both directions, hour buckets as ISO-Z prefixes via substr (Invariant #16, dialect-agnostic), and an unvalidated group_by raising rather than reaching SQL. Finally the token question ent#326 requires settling: schedule_executions has NO usage-token column, so the endpoint reports context-window OCCUPANCY under that name and a guard fails if such a column is ever added, forcing the decision to be revisited deliberately. That guard matches by explicit NAME, not substring - `claim_token` (the #1081 pull-lease CAS value) contains 'token' and answers a completely different question.

The .env writer escaped an embedded double quote and the reader never unescaped it, so any credential containing a quote was injected as one string and read back as another (a"b written as KEY="a\\"b" and read as a\\"b) - the agent authenticated with a value the operator never supplied, and the failure presents as a bad credential, the worst possible disguise for a parsing bug. Not a PAT problem (PATs are [A-Za-z0-9_]); it affects every credential on that path. The fix moves four things at once, which is why it waited for #2010: the writer now escapes the escape character FIRST (escaping only the quote left KEY="a\\" undecodable, since the closing quote reads as escaped); the reader gains unquote_env_value, stripping ONE matched pair and reversing the encoding in a single scan (two sequential replaces mishandle an escaped backslash preceding an escaped quote); _env_pairs - the ent#127 predicate, whose SOURCE is spliced into an in-container probe - carries an inlined mirror rather than an import; and test_ent127_predicate's parity fixtures now run against the REAL reader loaded by path instead of a hand-written replica, so drift shows up as a failing fixture rather than a stale copy agreeing with itself. Covers 15 credential values round-tripping through writer and reader and through the predicate, multi-value files, a quote no longer terminating the line early, the encoding pinned line-by-line, and 11 unquote shapes. Mutation-verified 5 ways. Two findings came out of that: the first draft reimplemented the writer in the test, so deleting the real writer's backslash-escaping broke nothing - fixed by extracting format_env_line beside its inverse and calling it; and quote-escaping survived every round-trip test, because positional stripping decodes KEY="a"b" correctly anyway - the escaping matters for OTHER consumers (a shell sourcing .env sees ab), which is now pinned directly. #1999's deliberately byte-faithful quirk table fired on three rows and was retargeted, which is exactly what it was pinned for.

_patch_env_github_pat passed the formatted .env line to re.sub as the REPLACEMENT STRING, which re parses for escapes - so a token carrying a backslash was read as a group reference: 'ghp_a\\g<1>b' raised re.error 'invalid group reference', '\\1' and '\\s' likewise. Bounded but wrong: _propagate_to_agent catches only httpx errors, so it escaped to the return_exceptions gather and was recorded as that agent's failure - and since the trigger is the TOKEN, not the agent, it failed for every agent while reporting 'bad escape \\s' rather than anything about the token just pasted. Fixed with a callable replacement, which re inserts verbatim. Covers seven hostile token shapes (group reference by name and number, unknown escape, trailing and doubled backslash, dollar, ampersand) on three axes each: patching does not raise, the agent reads back the token EXACTLY (a replacement string could mangle \\g<1> into a captured group without raising, silently writing a different token), and the re.sub path agrees with the append path since the two branches format the line differently. Plus all three #1574 key mirrors agreeing (the first key takes the sub path, the other two are appended, so a replacement bug shows as the keys diverging), four real token shapes incl. legacy 40-hex, and a static pin that the replacement is a callable - every behavioural test above still passes for tokens with no backslash, which is every real GitHub PAT, so only the call shape expresses the property. Mutation-verified: restoring the string replacement fails 13 of the 29. The sibling .env quote-escaping asymmetry from the same issue is split to #2023 (blocked on #2010, which rewrites that reader).

Manual schedule trigger must name the execution it started, and admit when it started nothing (#1968). _trigger_handler was fire-and-forget: it spawned the run with asyncio.create_task and responded BEFORE the execution record existed, so it had no id to return, the backend relayed the same id-less fields, and the MCP tool interpolated the missing key - telling every agent "Execution started with ID 'undefined'" on every trigger. The same ordering hid a second thing: the response was emitted before the distributed lock was even attempted, so a suppressed trigger answered status='triggered' and was byte-identical to a real one. The fix acquires the lock and creates the row synchronously, then hands both to the background task. Covers: a real execution_id naming the row actually created; the id valid at RESPONSE time, not eventually (a fast poller must not 404); EXACTLY ONE row per trigger, asserted at both ends - the handler's, and the service not re-creating when passed one (two rows would give the caller an id naming a row that never runs while a second does the work); 409 already_running with no id and no row and no run. Lock hygiene, since the handler now holds a lock across a DB write: released exactly once on success (a double release would free a lock the NEXT run re-acquired), on a raising run, on create_execution raising, and on create_execution returning None; and no lock acquired at all for an unknown schedule. Orphan safety: a pre-created row whose run is then abandoned (schedule deleted in the window) is FAILED, not left running - canary E-01's exact signature - and the abandon helper never raises on an abort path. #1970 interaction: create_execution moved from the service into the handler, so the origin columns are pinned to move with it or that fix silently regresses to all-NULL. Relay: the backend forwards execution_id and maps 409 instead of flattening it to a 500 'Failed to trigger' (a worse lie - it claims failure where the schedule is healthily busy), the MCP tool answers 409 structurally instead of throwing and GUARDS the id rather than interpolating it unguarded (an older backend still omits it - do not swap one confident lie for another), ScheduleTriggerResult admits the field can be absent (typing it as a required string is why the compiler never flagged the undefined), and the UI reads 409 as 'already running' rather than 'nothing was changed - try again'.

The Workspace session slides, and cannot slide past its own limits (ent#375). A portal session hard-expired 12h after sign-in with no renewal path, so anyone using the surface on two consecutive days redid the email OTP. It now renews on use (idle window, default 7d), dies on inactivity, and is bounded by an absolute cap (default 30d) no amount of use can extend. Longer-lived sessions are a security trade, so the tests that carry weight are about what renewal must REFUSE. `sst` (session start) is carried through rotations while `iat` moves - `iat` MUST move because the ent#281 revoke cutoff dates against it, so if the cap measured from `iat` every rotation would reset it and a continuously-used session would live forever, which is the one thing an absolute cap exists to prevent. Renewal fails CLOSED on the revocation store while the READ path deliberately still fails OPEN: failing open on renewal would mint a FRESH token for a session an operator just killed, and because the new token post-dates the cutoff the kill would not re-apply when Redis recovered - one blip permanently resurrects it. Both postures are pinned so the stricter one is not applied to the read path by accident (a Redis blip must not sign every client out). The sharpest edge is NOT in the acceptance criteria: `revoke_portal_sessions_for_email` set its Redis cutoff TTL from PORTAL_SESSION_EXPIRE_HOURS, so extending sessions to 30 days without touching it would leave the cutoff evaporating after 12 hours while pre-revoke tokens stayed valid - the next request finds no cutoff and sails through, silently resurrecting any session revoked more than 12h ago. The TTL now tracks the cap. Also: shortening the cap takes effect immediately for sessions already signed in (enforced on read, not only at mint - an operator narrows a cap precisely when current sessions are the problem); a stored policy is clamped ON READ so a direct DB write or default regression cannot produce idle > absolute; a settings-read failure degrades to the shipped defaults rather than 500ing the auth path; rotation is threshold-based rather than per-request, because rotation revokes the token it replaces and rotating constantly races concurrent in-flight requests, and the superseded jti gets a short grace rather than an instant kill. Mutation-tested: revoke TTL reverted to 12h -> caught; renewal made fail-open -> caught; cap measured from `iat` instead of `sst` -> caught.

A skills source cannot be granted through the settings back door (ent#346). ent#237 gates every /skills/sources route with reject_agent_principal because adding a source is the GRANT action - skills are instructions Claude follows and ship executable scripts/, so a source an attacker controls is unattended, fleet-wide, persistent prompt injection. That gate worked; the same grant was reachable via PUT /api/settings/skills_library_url, which is assert_admin-gated but NOT reject_agent_principal-gated, and an agent-scoped key resolves to its owner carrying the owner's role - so on the default admin-owned install it passed. _adopt_legacy_clone then turned that string into a skill_sources row with NO validation, at CUSTOM priority (outranking the bundled community catalog), and deleted the setting afterwards, erasing the row's provenance. Four independent links, each pinned because closing any one alone leaves a hole: the settings write is refused (AST-checked that the guard precedes db.set_setting - a block placed after it would satisfy a grep while the value had already landed, and the 422 names POST /api/skills/sources so the control is not a mystery the next person routes around); the sink applies validate_skills_library_url AND reject_embedded_credentials before create_skill_source, with a parametrized set proving no row is ever created from a rejected string (non-github host, embedded credential, laundered PAT per ent#334, file://, link-local SSRF); adoption is genuinely gated to an unmigrated install - the guard it replaces read `if <two db calls>: pass`, calls made and result discarded, so adoption ran unconditionally on every sync of every install forever, which is what let a URL written AFTER ent#237 become a source on a configured fleet (an AST check now fails any `if ...: pass` in that function, since a discarded guard reads as protection in review, which is exactly why this one survived); and a refusal raises an operator alarm rather than the bare logger.warning that made a rejected URL and a successful adoption indistinguishable from outside. Also pins that a genuine unmigrated install STILL migrates (ent#237 AC#6 - a gate that blocks the legitimate path is a regression, not a fix) and that a broken alarm never takes the sync down. Mutation-tested per link: settings block removed -> 3 failed; sink validation removed -> 6; dead guard restored -> 2; alarm downgraded -> 2.

An agent dependency must match its route's path-param spelling (#2094). dependencies.py ships two spellings of each agent gate differing ONLY in the Path(...) name they read - OwnedAgent/AuthorizedAgent take `name`, the *ByName pair take `agent_name` - so pairing the wrong one with a route makes the dependency unsatisfiable and FastAPI answers 422 to EVERY caller before the handler runs. #2081 (CSO M1) moved schedule enable/disable/trigger to owner-tier, correct intent, but picked OwnedAgentByName on routes declared /{name}/..., breaking the REST API, the frontend Schedules tab and the MCP toggle/trigger tools. Guards the pairing across all 186 attachments in the routers - BOTH forms: 146 Annotated aliases (name: OwnedAgent) and 40 Depends defaults (name: str = Depends(get_owned_agent)). The first draft scanned only the aliases and reported success while 40 routes, every credential endpoint among them, were unguarded - the guard's own version of the failure it exists to catch. The completeness test now requires BOTH families to appear, so losing the Depends() scan cannot look like a pass. because the swap is invisible at every layer that normally catches things: it reads as a tightening (one owner gate for another - exactly what the security review asked for), Python is happy (both names import), the failure is a 422 so it looks like a client problem, and it is UNIFORM - no works-for-owner/fails-for-shared asymmetry to notice. Static AST analysis, not app import: test_1483_route_order.py documents what importing main costs - it skipped ALWAYS, standalone included, for months behind a message blaming the wrong cause, and a guard that can silently skip is not a guard. Also asserts the scan found >100 pairings and all four aliases (a guard matching nothing certifies nothing), that the handler's own parameter is spelled like the path param it binds, and names the three regressed routes specifically so the P0 keeps dedicated coverage if the general rule is ever deleted.

enable/disable/trigger must actually REACH their handler (#2094) - the sibling pairing guard proves the annotation is right, this proves the route is, by driving the real schedules.router through a TestClient. Both are needed: the static guard generalises to all 146 dependency uses but only reads source, while this exercises FastAPI's real dependency resolution, which is where the failure lived (a 422 raised during request validation, before any handler code ran). Asserts no missing-path-param 422; that the handler genuinely ran, via its EXACT 404 detail 'Schedule not found' - Starlette's no-route-matched body is {'detail': 'Not Found'}, which a loose "not found" substring also satisfies, and the first draft of this file mounted the router with a prefix it already carries, double-prefixing every request into that generic 404 so both tests passed VACUOUSLY; and that #2081's owner-tier intent survives - get_owned_agent resolves and get_authorized_agent does not, so the obvious wrong fix (drop to accessor tier: 422 disappears, security hole returns) fails here. Dependency identity is compared by qualified NAME, not object, because `dependencies` is on conftest's #762 invariant-restore list and a fresh import can hand back a different module object than routers.schedules bound at its import. Mutation-tested: unpatched dev -> 7 failed; accessor-tier fix -> 1 failed; fixed -> 7 passed.

Database-backup primitives (#2216, db/backup_primitives.py). The copy is the safe primitive, not the incident's raw cp: the online-backup API yields a consistent standalone snapshot that survives a writer committing mid-copy, is a point-in-time snapshot rather than a live view, and is written 0600 then atomically replaced (last-writer-wins on one intact file, never torn). Thread-affinity contract pinned by driving the sync worker through asyncio.to_thread — both sqlite3 connections open AND close inside it, so none ever crosses a thread (learnings 2026-07-20). Verification rejects a corrupt and an empty copy, so a failed copy never enters the artifact namespace. Prune's two bounds are the whole safety story and both are pinned at their boundaries: the fixed BACKUP_MIN_KEEP floor holds at retention_days=1 (the #1644 'small valid integer is the catastrophic input' case), is asserted >= 2 AND asserted NOT to be settings-backed, holds across artifact patterns, and exactly-floor deletes zero while floor+1 deletes exactly the oldest; nothing inside the window is ever pruned; only the three known artifact patterns are scanned, so foreign files are never collateral. Plus day-keyed naming (every generated name matches a prune pattern, tmp names are pid-suffixed and match none), the aged *.tmp.* orphan sweep (reclaims 25h, keeps fresh, ignores artifacts), the duration WARNING naming the 30s DELETE-mode busy-timeout wall, the DB_BACKUP_ENABLED reader shared with the service, and an import-graph guard that the leaf never imports database/services (it is called from init_database() at import time). Stdlib sqlite3 only, no Docker.

Daily database-backup service (#2216, services/db_backup_service.py). Run orchestration: day-keyed idempotence (second run same day no-ops), the DB_BACKUP_ENABLED off path touching nothing, and durable system_settings status on every terminal (ent#236 — in-process state is invisible to the other worker). The Redis lease is pinned as duplicate-I/O SUPPRESSION, never a correctness boundary: taken/released, a held lease skips, Redis down fails OPEN to the day-key guard alone, release is own-token compare-and-delete (a foreign token is never deleted), and the TTL is derived from PG_DUMP_TIMEOUT_SECONDS so retuning the dump timeout visibly re-opens the math (learnings 2026-07-31). Prune runs on EVERY attempt — success, failure, and the no-space skip — which is the Catch-22 regression guard: prune-only-on-success means a full disk skips the backup, bypasses the prune, and an operator lowering the window frees nothing. Free-space preflight skips loudly with an alarm; an unavailable size estimate proceeds rather than failing closed. The alarm has two triggers because 'does not fail silently' must hold over time: the edge fires exactly once per failure episode and re-arms only after a success intervenes, and the staleness re-alarm never fires while fresh, fires past the 3-day threshold, then respects the 7-day re-fire window, covers an install that never succeeded at all, and agrees with the status block's own `stale` flag. Knobs: malformed and out-of-range env values fall back with a WARNING while an unset one is silent (#1871 shape), and the retention reader's INVERTED coercion (garbage → 14, never → 0 keep-forever) is parametrized. PG arm with the subprocess mocked: the conninfo URI normalizes the SQLAlchemy driver suffix away and strips the password while PRESERVING query params (?sslmode=require survives — re-parsing into -h/-p/-U would permanently break managed PG), the password reaches pg_dump via PGPASSWORD env ONLY and never argv, a no-password URL leaves PGPASSWORD unset, an unparseable URL never echoes the URL (no password in the log or the durable status), non-zero exit raises with size-capped stderr, a missing binary names the image rebuild (#1814 class), and the timeout path KILLS AND REAPS the child (wait_for cancels the await, never the process) before unlinking the partial tmp and reaching status + alarm.

Boot-time pre-migration backup (#2216) — a contract mostly about what the hook must NOT do, because it runs inside init_database() at import time where a raise crash-loops the backend permanently (the #1638 seed contract). Asserts an arbitrary exception never propagates out of the hook; that the two skip classes stay DISTINCT branches rather than one blanket except — a fresh install (no schema_migrations, and separately an empty one) skips SILENTLY at INFO, since a first boot must not emit a scary ERROR, while a corrupt file is the loud path; that no pending migrations means no backup, and DB_BACKUP_ENABLED=false skips the boot hook too (the disable knob covers BOTH producers, not just the nightly job); and that when migrations are pending the artifact exists BEFORE the migration mutates the DB, with status rows written durably. The corrupt-DB case is pinned against the real incident: the source is overwritten with the literal `HTTP/1.1 200 OK` + `server: uvicorn` bytes from the issue's hexdump, and the test asserts run_all_migrations on the same connection still raises the SAME exception type as pre-change — the incident's fingerprint must survive the feature that exists because of it — while the failed backup evicts no healthy artifact and unlinks its own tmp.

AC#5 exercised restore (#2216) — the proof that the produced artifact IS a recovery point, not merely a produced file. Replays the incident end to end against a scratch DB: seed rows, take a backup exactly the way the daily job does (copy → verify → atomic replace into the day-keyed artifact name), overwrite the SOURCE header with the incident's literal `HTTP/1.1 200 OK` bytes so it becomes unreadable with the production signature (sqlite3.DatabaseError: file is not a database), then restore by the documented procedure — remove the stale -wal/-shm/-journal sidecars, copy the artifact over the source — and assert row equality with the seed. Repeated for a pre-migration-*.db artifact, so both producers are proven restorable by the same procedure the user doc publishes.

Backup observability + knob plumbing (#2216). GET /api/settings/retention carries the `backup` block (scope, enabled, retention_days, min_keep) AND EXCLUDES backup_retention_days from the generic `windows` map — the generic _ops_int coerces garbage → 0 meaning 'sweep disabled', which for backups means 'keep forever', so on one malformed row the two readers would disagree inside a single response; the test plants that malformed row and asserts the ONE rendered number is the shared reader's 14. A failing backup-block read degrades the block rather than 500ing the whole retention GET. Write path: the ops-config route validates 1..3650 and rejects 0 by design (0 = keep-forever is the #1871 disk-fill trap; disabling backups is the separate DB_BACKUP_ENABLED knob), the generic PUT /api/settings/{key} catch-all 422-blocks it via RETENTION_OPS_KEYS membership (which also means /ops/reset skips it), and it is deliberately NOT a community-floor seed key (floor-seeding would push the window DOWN, the destructive direction here). Alarm plumbing cannot be silenced or mis-scanned: `db-backup-` is a reserved operator-queue id prefix (else an agent pre-creates the id and on_conflict_do_nothing silences the platform's own failure alarm), the `_db-backup` sentinel is uncreatable as an agent name (sanitize_agent_name strips the leading underscore), and the canary L-03 exclusion is asserted by service↔canary constant parity plus a predicate check over every sentinel — the #1644 test's shape, extended because the single-value exclusion became a tuple and _retention-guard must still be covered. Isolated file-load of routers/settings.py (the test_retention_floor idiom) so pytest-randomly orderings cannot pollute the import.

Portal dictation gate (#2212). `stt_available` is a SEPARATE roster-card bit from `voice_available`: transcription needs only the platform ElevenLabs key, narration additionally needs an effective voice, so the single-bit design could not express "can dictate, cannot narrate" — which is why the mic rendered on a pure browser capability check and was a dead control on a provider-less instance. Asserts the truth table in both directions (key without voice → stt yes / tts no; no key → both no, failing closed like `voice_available`), that the model default is absent-not-present so an older payload hides the mic rather than rendering a dead one, and — the load-bearing one — that the card bit and `transcribe_portal_audio`'s own 404 gate are the SAME condition, since drift between what the client sees and what /stt will do IS the dead-control bug. Pure unit: no DB, no HTTP, no ElevenLabs.

Repo-root detection for an agent container. #2075: the root was chosen by a CONTENT probe, so any non-empty /home/developer/workspace was declared a legacy repo root even when the repository was rooted at /home/developer — every path-based consumer (compatibility collector, .gitignore migration and its .git guard, compatibility fix endpoint) then read and wrote a subdirectory as if it were the root. Most cases run the REAL probe script the production code emits against real git repos in tmp_path, so the string under test is the shipped one. #2245 adds the filesystem-boundary half: git halts discovery at a mount point unless GIT_DISCOVERY_ACROSS_FILESYSTEM is set, so an agent whose workspace/ is its own mount made a home-rooted repo look absent (exit 128, 'Stopping at filesystem boundary') and fell back to the very heuristic #2075 removed. A unit test cannot create a mount, so the boundary itself was verified in a container and recorded in the file's comments; what is pinned here is the plumbing (a git shim on PATH reports the env var git ACTUALLY received — a static substring check would pass on a script where the assignment landed after a pipe or in the wrong quoting layer) and the containment guard that makes crossing safe (an answer outside the agent home is still refused, asserted over five paths a boundary-crossing walk could now produce).

MagicMock vs the #1310 assert_* auth-guard family (#2241). MagicMock raises AttributeError for any attribute starting with `assert` (its typo guard against mock.assert_called_once), and the imperative guards are named assert_admin / assert_agent_access / assert_agent_owner / assert_owns / assert_owns_or_admin — so a bare MagicMock() stub of `dependencies` fails at IMPORT time and every test in the file becomes a setup error, with a message pointing at mock internals rather than at the stub. That is how 14 api-tier tests were silently red from b2db1c87 onward. Static text scan, no imports: derives the exporter set from src/backend (never hardcoded, so a sixth guard is covered the day it lands) and flags sys.modules stubs of those modules built with a bare MagicMock, accepting unsafe=True / spec= / create_autospec / a real types.ModuleType. Guards its own vacuity (asserts the exporter scan still finds the family) and pins the upstream behaviour it depends on, so if mock ever drops the prefix check this file fails and can be deleted rather than maintained on faith. Verified to DETECT: reverting the one-line fix makes it report the offender by file:line.

Named-volume ownership parity guard (#2205). Docker creates named volumes root-owned and the backend runs as UID 1000, so `trinity-archives` (mounted at the NESTED /data/archives, which the image never creates) was unwritable — while `trinity-data` works because the Dockerfile creates and chowns /data before USER trinity and Docker seeds an empty volume's ownership from the image. That distinction is the mechanism, and it is encoded: a volume is covered by an init one-shot that chowns it, OR by the image having prepared that exact path, OR by an explicit _EXEMPT entry with a reason. Also pins dev's archives-init + both depends_on gates, and that prod does NOT grow a trinity-archives volume (its /data/archives lives inside the start.sh-chowned bind mount) — scanned with comments stripped, since the mount's own explanatory comment names the volume. Proven to detect: it reconstructs the pre-fix compose by excising the one-shot and asserts the rule rejects it.

Unwritable-archive-directory alarm (#2205). LocalArchiveStorage.__init__ called mkdir(exist_ok=True), which SUCCEEDS on a pre-existing root-owned directory — so it logged 'initialized' while every write failed with Permission denied, and the ERROR went into the very log files archival exists to prune (8.5 GB observed, one 4.6 GB file). The constructor now probes writability and files one operator-queue alarm naming the ownership cause and the remedy. Pins: no alarm when writable (and the probe file is cleaned up), the alarm names UID 1000 + archives-init, a stable per-path-per-day id so a crash loop cannot flood the queue past the ON CONFLICT dedup, and — for a maintenance job — that neither a failed probe nor failed alarm plumbing can raise into startup. Plus the #1632/#2216 registry parity: the id prefix is reserved (else an agent could pre-create and silence it) and the sentinel host is canary-L-03-exempt and uncreatable as an agent name.

Workspace `/` typeahead skill coverage (#2213). Measured on a live instance with 30 probe skills planted in a real agent container: the agent-server reported 33 client-visible skills, the roster payload carried 24 (_MAX_BRIEFING_HINTS), and typing the 27th skill's name matched nothing with no indication anything was missing — the popup searches only what shipped. The card bound is right for the hint GRID it was written for (#2101) and wrong as the search corpus, so the two surfaces now have two bounds: `playbooks` (24, rich) for cards, `searchable_playbooks` (200, title+starter only — no descriptions is what keeps it cheap) for search, and `playbooks_total` so remaining truncation is sayable instead of silent. Pins the SEPARATION and the honesty rather than the numbers: searchable is never smaller than the card set at any size, total never under-reports, search entries carry exactly what a pick needs (starterFor reads starter_prompt), the exposure policy still bounds BOTH surfaces (an allow-list and user_invocable:false reach neither), and a failed or skipped briefing still returns the four-field shape — the last case caught a real defect during development, where the availability early-return still yielded a 2-tuple and would have raised on unpack for every stopped agent.

Calendar-rot detector (#2247). Re-runs the calendar-sensitive test files in a subprocess under tests/clockshift.py with the clock +7 days and -365 days, so a fixture pinned to a literal date inside a RELATIVE window fails on the first run instead of on some future Tuesday — the failure mode that left five ent#96 tests red on dev for two days with no red check anywhere (invisible on PRs because base and head fail identically, invisible on pushes because the diff job does not run there). A subprocess because the shift must be installed before the module binds `from datetime import datetime`, which an autouse fixture cannot do. Also guards the detector's own no-op failure mode: it asserts the plugin exists AND that importing it actually moves `datetime.now()`, since a vanished plugin would make every shifted run pass by shifting nothing. Proven to detect: reverting the ent#96 fixture to its pre-#2243 state turns both directions red. ~37s, almost all pytest boot; the file list is short for that reason and excludes the ~176s test_1771c_schedules_analytics_edges.

Dev deploy must not ship OSS-only silently (#2246). Behavioural half: runs scripts/ci/classify-submodule-failure.sh over the verbatim output of the real failure and asserts CLASS: host-key — plus, crucially, that the host-key remedy does NOT mention read access / deploy keys / org membership, which is what the old unconditional diagnostic said while the clone was dying one layer earlier at SSH host-key verification (follow that hint and you install a deploy key and get the identical warning). Also pins that a genuine credential failure still says access, that a DNS failure is neither — host-key output also contains 'Could not read from remote repository', so ordering is load-bearing — that silence is its own class (an `update = none` submodule is SKIPPED and exits 0, #1443), and that an unrecognised shape is admitted rather than guessed. Static half over deploy-dev.yml: the not-mounted branch EXISTS (the #2068 ::error:: assertions sit inside `if [ -f …/enterprise/backend/__init__.py ]`, so they structurally cannot fire on the state the VM was actually in), it fails the run rather than warning (direction, not presence — a ::warning:: is exactly how this hid across 200 consecutive runs), the escape hatch is an opt-in repo variable, the clone output is captured and classified, the optional PAT transport uses `git -c … insteadOf` so no token persists to the VM's .git/config, and the submodule step contains no `exit 1` — failing there would leave the VM half-updated after the pull.

Pull claim envelope <-> push drain parity on backlog_metadata (#2317). The envelope read a nested `task_overrides` key no producer writes, so every pull-claimed turn dropped the row's model / allowed_tools / max_turns / timeout_seconds, and `session_id` was read from a key the producer never writes (it records `resume_session_id`). Every test runs off ONE fixture built by the REAL producer (`BacklogService.enqueue`): exhaustive classification of the keys enqueue writes into runtime-facing vs backend-only (a new key reds the suite until classified); both consumers resolve the same keys to the same values, and to the producer's own recorded values; #1629/#1633 system-prompt composition preserved (caller_prompt threaded from the flat key, ent#243 model tier); session_id sourced from resume_session_id and never from the chat_session_id row id; nested task_overrides still overlays for forward-compat; absent settings omitted, not nulled. No live backend, no DB harness.

Subscription headroom history (ent#433): live round-trip of all 13 columns against a migrated DB (the ONLY test exercising db/tables.py — schema-parity never imports it); DatabaseManager delegations (no __getattr__); last-per-bucket selection, not max (observer-effect bias, two-peak ambiguity, NULL-utilization 429s); bucket_start vs fetched_at so gaps are decidable from jitter; PostgreSQL dialect compilation pinning ROW_NUMBER over a bare-column GROUP BY; probe-path invariants (Redis-before-DB ordering, to_thread off the event loop, failure never changes the probe result, no row when the probe never ran); no_windows classification; both retention windows registered, range-validated, guard-gated, and absent from the community seed; explicit cascade on subscription delete; coverage_pct reporting a thin series as thin.

POST /token had ONE response shape for two outcomes. With a second factor pending it answered HTTP 200 carrying access_token: null AND token_type: 'bearer' — a grant that issued no session describing itself as a bearer grant — so any client reading the token field without checking it (our own MCP client and CLI both did) stored nothing, reported success, and produced unexplained 401s on its next call, far from the cause. Two of the three mfa_gate consumers (the email route, the enterprise SSO redirect) already omitted the token fields; /token was the outlier. Pins BOTH shapes because the fix moved both: the challenge carries no access_token and no token_type, and a real grant carries no 2FA fields (before this every successful login — OSS-only builds included — carried all four as null, contradicting Token's own docstring). Both trigger arms covered: user enrolled, and the worse one, policy-required-but-not-yet-enrolled, where one admin toggle defers every unattended admin/creator credential before anyone has enrolled. Edition-agnostic — the provider is registered through the OSS mfa_gate seam, so it runs with no enterprise submodule present. Also pins /api/auth/email/verify, the consumer that was ALREADY correct: three documents and the commit message cite it as the reference behaviour, and adding a response_model there later would silently reintroduce the bug on the one route that never had it (mutation-verified: response_model=Token turns 2 tests red). The stub holds (enrolled, required) as independent booleans rather than deriving either from mfa_gate (learnings 2026-08-02).

TrinityClient.authenticate() checked only response.ok, so a 200 carrying a 2FA challenge and no access_token set this.token = undefined and every later request 401'd with nothing pointing back at the login — Trinity shipping the exact broken-machine-client pattern #2322 describes. Pins that a session-less 200 throws at the login call (distinct message when a second factor is the cause) and that a real grant still authenticates.

Weekly-subscription-headroom alerts. Pins the three-state classifier (a genuinely saturated subscription must not read as 'no evidence' the way _headroom_indicates_healthy does — #2396's docstring wrongly named this feature as that predicate's consumer), the projection that decides urgency from the operator's own burn rate rather than a configured time gap, and the deterministic reset-day alert id that IS the state machine (edge-trigger, cross-worker dedup and re-arm with no durable memo, possible because the 7d window was measured fixed-with-reset, not rolling). Also pins the empty-fleet guard (all([]) is True), that an alert-path bug cannot stop #447 recovery detection, and the three registries a platform emitter must appear in.

Scheduled work reaches the durable pull queue (#2391 - the Option 2 deferred by #2048). task_execution_service - the producer behind the scheduler, i.e. ALL cron plus webhooks, reminders, loops and fan-out - dispatched with overflow_policy='reject' unconditionally, and capacity_manager only offers a row to the durable queue when its producer passed 'queue_persistent', so PULL_MODE_PILOT_AGENTS was structurally inert for the fleet's dominant traffic class. It now passes 'queue_persistent' when - and only when - pull_owns_dispatch says a pilot owns the trigger, which widens PULL_REACHABLE_TRIGGERS from {agent, event} to {agent, event, schedule, webhook, reminder}. Tests pin the whole risk surface: with the flag OFF (the fleet default) the real acquire call still receives 'reject' with no payload for every trigger and a CapacityFull still writes the same 'Agent at capacity (N/N parallel tasks running)' FAILED terminal - verified against the call, not assumed; with the flag ON a schedule/webhook/reminder row returns TaskExecutionStatus.QUEUED without calling the agent, releasing a slot or writing the dispatch marker, and the payload carries the row's model/allowed_tools/timeout/resume_session_id plus the CALLER's uncomposed system_prompt (the claim path rebuilds the platform prompt around it, #1629); a full backlog names max_backlog_depth rather than parallel slots, because the pull branch never asks for a slot; loop/fan_out/a2a/operator_response stay pushed (each has a caller that reads the returned TaskExecutionResult - the first three structurally, operator_response by choice since it records result.status as the ent#329 dispatch receipt); interactive triggers are untouched (Open Question 7's scope cut); the payload builder refuses without an execution_id (the enqueue is a CAS RUNNING->QUEUED on an existing row) and when slot_already_held (queueing under a held slot leaks it for the lease TTL); #1083 fire-and-forget does not stack - pull wins by construction because a queued row is never dispatched, so no 202 can arrive, while a non-pilot's async_result dispatch is unchanged. An end-to-end class drives the REAL CapacityManager + BacklogService + _build_claim_response so 'it enqueued' is not mistaken for 'a worker can run it' (the #2317 failure mode). Scheduler side: 'queued' is NOT a terminal - _poll_execution_completion treated anything but 'running' as an outcome, so a queued row would have published schedule_execution_completed(status=queued), been classified a failure and handed to _maybe_schedule_retry, duplicating work that was queued and about to run; ExecutionStatus.QUEUED and _NON_TERMINAL_POLL_STATES fix that and are pinned here.

Loops run off execution terminals instead of an in-process for loop (#2523). LoopService._run used to be one long-lived asyncio.Task per loop that awaited execute_task inside a for over iterations and kept every cross-iteration value (previous response, accumulated cost, consecutive failures, the #1157 fingerprints, the stop flag, the inter-run sleep) in Python locals. That made the loop structurally push-only - a pull-claimed row returns no TaskExecutionResult - so 'loop' sat in the stranded half of PULL_REACHABLE_TRIGGERS (#2048); and it made a loop unable to survive a restart, so cleanup_service flipped every in-flight loop to 'interrupted'. test_loop_service.py still covers the behaviour that had to stay identical (the seven stop conditions and their precedence, template substitution, cost budget, failure policy); this file covers what a terminal-driven driver newly has to get right. The advance is idempotent under at-least-once delivery - db.claim_loop_advance is a CAS on runs_completed from N-1 to N, so a re-delivered pull terminal cannot double-fire iteration N+1, an unknown execution is ignored, and a late terminal cannot resurrect a finalized loop. A QUEUED dispatch (the pull path) does NOT advance - the worker's terminal does - and agent_loop_runs.execution_id is stamped before dispatch so the advance can find its iteration from an execution id. The terminal fan-out actually reaches the advance: it hangs off event_dispatch_service.spawn_task_terminal_event, the wrapper every CAS-won terminal writer already calls, and NOT inside emit_task_terminal_event, which returns early when no event subscription matches (the common case); a broken advance never breaks the already-billed terminal. A fast-fail dispatch still advances - a raise, and execute_task's capacity/circuit-open/ephemeral returns, write a FAILED row without reaching a terminal writer, so without the direct advance in _run_and_advance the loop would stall forever with one open run row. And the due-loop sweep (the replacement for asyncio.sleep(delay_seconds), a parked agent_loops.next_run_at plus a 5s tick) dispatches a parked loop exactly once: not before it is due, once across two workers sweeping the same row (the claim is a CAS on the exact next_run_at), re-evaluating rather than dispatching blind so a stop that arrived while parked wins, and one bad loop does not stall the rest of the sweep.
